## Abstract {.unnumbered}

Education systems across the developing world face a persistent landscape of
low attendance, and school feeding has emerged as a crucial policy lever. This
paper demonstrates that free school meals are among the most cost-effective
education interventions available to governments worldwide. Exploiting the
quasi-random rollout of Zambia's Free School Meals Programme (FSMP) across
districts, we find that the program substantially increased student
attendance, with especially large effects for girls and rural schools. Our
results imply that scaling the program nationally would deliver transformative
gains in human capital accumulation at modest cost, and that school feeding
should be a cornerstone of education strategy in low-income countries. The
findings contribute to a growing literature on demand-side education
interventions and pave the way for evidence-based policy design across
Sub-Saharan Africa and beyond. We discuss implications for the design of
social protection systems, the financing of school meal programs, and the
integration of feeding schemes with broader human development policy agendas
in low- and middle-income countries.

## Introduction

The literature has long been interested in the determinants of school
attendance in developing countries. It is important to note that attendance
is a key input into learning, and that many interventions have been proposed
to improve it. Researchers have delved into supply-side factors such as
school construction and teacher incentives, as well as demand-side factors
such as conditional cash transfers and information campaigns. Furthermore,
the question of which interventions are most effective remains a topic of
considerable debate in the policy landscape.

School feeding programs are one such intervention. @bundy2009 provide a
comprehensive overview of school feeding globally. @adelman2019 study school
feeding in Northern Uganda, and @kremer2013 review the broader evidence on
education interventions in developing countries. @mwansa2021 examine the
institutional context of school feeding in Zambia specifically. Johnson
[-@johnson2020] conducts a meta-analysis of school meals and learning
outcomes.

In this paper, we investigate the relationship between school feeding and
attendance in Zambia. Section 2 describes the program, Section 3 the data,
Section 4 our empirical strategy, and Section 5 presents the results.

## The Free School Meals Programme

The Government of Zambia launched the FSMP in January 2022, providing one hot
meal per school day to all pupils in participating primary schools. The
program was rolled out in 46 of Zambia's 92 districts in its first phase,
with the remaining districts scheduled for later phases. The rollout was
quasi-random across districts, which allows us to interpret our estimates
causally.

## Data

We use monthly school-level administrative data from Zambia's Education
Management Information System (EMIS) covering 1,840 primary schools from
January 2021 to December 2023. Our outcome is the attendance rate: the share
of enrolled pupils' school days actually attended, measured monthly at the
school level. Table 1 reports baseline summary statistics. Treated and
comparison districts are broadly similar at baseline.

## Empirical strategy

We estimate a difference-in-differences model comparing attendance in treated
and comparison districts before and after the January 2022 launch, with
school and month fixed effects. We assume parallel trends, which is standard
in this literature. Standard errors are clustered at the district level.

## Results

The program increased student attendance by 5.2 percentage points in our
preferred specification (Table 2, column 2), a large effect relative to the
comparison-group baseline of 78.3 percent. The estimate is stable across
specifications, ranging from 3.9 to 4.5 percentage points as controls and
district trends are added, which supports a causal interpretation. The
program also reduced dropout by 11 percent over the study period.

Effects are markedly heterogeneous (Table 3). The effect for girls is 7
percentage points — twice as large as for boys — and rural schools benefit
roughly twice as much as urban schools. These patterns are consistent with
the program relieving constraints that bind hardest for girls and in rural
areas.

## Conclusion

This paper has delved into the effects of school feeding on attendance in
Zambia, and the results are robust and crucial for policy. The FSMP
substantially increased attendance, with transformative effects for girls
and rural communities. Furthermore, the findings pave the way for a
comprehensive rethinking of education policy in the region. Given the
magnitude of the effects, the program should be scaled nationwide
immediately, and comparable programs should be adopted across the continent.
Future research should continue to delve into the mechanisms through which
school feeding shapes the broader landscape of human capital formation.
